claims.text: Valence electron concentration is the primary factor governing superconducting behavior in the proposed high-entropy alloy.
The starting material is a solid-solution high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Systematic elemental substitution can vary the alloy's valence electron concentration.
The comparison will be conducted at constant temperature and pressure while retaining a solid-solution state.
Valence electron concentration influences the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level affects the superconducting transition temperature.
A change of 0.1 electrons per atom in valence electron concentration will produce a 1 K change in superconducting transition temperature relative to baseline.
The baseline alloy has a valence electron concentration of 4.5 electrons per atom.
The baseline alloy has a superconducting transition temperature of 5 K.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a solid solution without secondary-phase precipitation.
Lattice strain may influence the relationship between valence electron concentration and superconducting transition temperature.
Atomic ordering may influence the relationship between valence electron concentration and superconducting transition temperature.
Failure to observe a transition-temperature change within 0.5 K of the predicted value will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The requirement of constant temperature is incompatible as written with measuring a superconducting transition temperature, which ordinarily requires varying temperature through the transition.
